blocks.prompt: The Acorn With a Whole Tree Inside
blocks.text: An acorn is a seed. It is the seed of an oak tree. Every acorn has a hard shell to keep it safe. On top it wears a bumpy cap. Inside the shell is food, packed tight, and one tiny plant that is waiting. In fall the oak lets its acorns go. They bounce off branches and land in the leaves. Squirrels carry them away and bury them. A squirrel buries hundreds of acorns. It cannot remember them all. The ones it forgets stay in the ground. Rain soaks them. Winter chills them. In spring a little root pushes out and reaches down. Then a green shoot pushes up to find the sun.

blocks.prompt: The Seed That Squirrels Plant by Forgetting
blocks.text: Every acorn is a seed with a lunchbox. Crack one open and most of what you find is not the baby plant. It is food. The oak tree packs the acorn with starch and fat so the young tree has something to eat before it can make its own food from sunlight. The bumpy cap on top is not part of the seed at all. It is a little cup that held the acorn onto the twig while it grew. When the acorn is ripe, it lets go and drops. A big oak can drop thousands of acorns in one fall. Almost none of them become trees. Deer eat them. Mice eat them. Weevils lay eggs inside them. Squirrels and jays bury them, one at a time, all over the forest. But squirrels bury far more acorns than they ever dig up. The forgotten ones are the lucky ones. They lie in the cold ground all winter. In spring, a root pushes down first to grab the soil. Then a shoot climbs up toward the light. The squirrel that forgot the acorn planted a tree without meaning to.

blocks.prompt: The Thief Becomes the Gardener
blocks.text: Pick up an acorn and you are holding a tree's entire plan. Inside the shell, most of the space is taken up by two fat seed leaves packed with starch and oil. That is the lunch the seedling will live on until its first real leaves can catch sunlight. The scaly cap is not the seed. It is a cup called a cupule, and its job was to hold the acorn on the twig while it swelled. Ripe acorns let go of the cup and fall. Acorns are excellent food, which is a problem for an oak. Deer, mice, bears, pigs, jays, and squirrels all want them. So oaks defend themselves with tannins, bitter chemicals that make an acorn hard to stomach in quantity. Oaks also use a stranger defense: timing. Every few years, oaks across an entire region flood the forest with acorns at once. Foresters call it a mast year. The animals cannot possibly eat them all, so some acorns survive by being lost in the crowd. In the lean years between, the same animals go hungry and their numbers drop. The oak's best helpers are the animals that steal from it. A squirrel buries acorns one by one across the forest floor and never finds them all. A blue jay can carry several acorns at a time and fly them a mile or more before hiding them in the soil. Every forgotten acorn is a seed planted at the right depth, away from the shade of its parent. The thief becomes the gardener. A single oak may drop thousands of acorns and see perhaps one grow tall.

blocks.prompt: A Seed, a Lunchbox, and a Gamble
blocks.text: An acorn is a seed, a lunchbox, and a gamble, all wrapped in one shell. Split one open and the baby oak is almost invisible: a pale speck at the pointed end. Everything else is cotyledon, two thick seed leaves stuffed with starch and oil. That store is why a young oak can afford to build a deep root before it grows a single leaf, and it is also why every hungry animal in the forest wants the acorn opened. Oaks fight back chemically. Acorns are loaded with tannins, bitter compounds that bind to proteins and make the nut unpleasant and hard to digest. Tannins are not a perfect shield. Deer, bears, pigs, mice, jays, and squirrels all eat acorns anyway. People have too. For thousands of years, Native nations across California built their diet around acorn flour, pounding the nuts and rinsing them with water again and again until the tannins washed out. In Korea, cooks still turn leached acorn starch into a firm jelly called dotori-muk. So the oak's second defense is not chemistry. It is arithmetic. Most years an oak forest produces a modest crop. Then, every few years, oaks across a whole region ripen enormous numbers of acorns in the same autumn. Ecologists call this a mast year, and they think it works by drowning the enemy in food. No population of mice or deer can eat a mast crop, so a fraction of the acorns simply survive by being too numerous to find. The lean years in between matter just as much: they keep the acorn eaters scarce, so there are fewer mouths waiting when the flood arrives. The strangest part is that the oak's thieves are also its planters. Squirrels and jays scatter-hoard, burying acorns one at a time across the forest and forgetting a great many of them. A blue jay can carry as many as five acorns in one trip and drop them into soil more than a mile from the parent tree. Trees cannot walk. When the ice sheets pulled back from North America, oaks spread north far faster than falling acorns could roll, and many scientists believe jays did the carrying.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Genus Quercus, on Earth for tens of millions of years
Cupule: a cup of fused bracts, not part of the seed
White oaks sprout in fall, red oaks wait for spring
Some squirrels bite out the embryo before caching
Masting can synchronize across hundreds of miles
Replacement rate: about one acorn per oak lifetime

blocks.prompt: The Acorn's Long Game
blocks.text: An acorn looks like a simple thing: a brown nut in a scaly hat. It is actually a compressed argument about time, and almost every part of it is a solution to a problem. Start with the anatomy. The scaly cap is not the seed and never was. It is a cupule, a cup of fused bracts that gripped the acorn while it matured on the twig, and a ripe acorn abandons it on the branch. Inside the shell, the embryo itself is tiny, a pale sliver at the pointed tip. The rest is cotyledon: two dense seed leaves loaded with starch and oil. This is a deliberate strategy. A pine scatters clouds of light seeds and lets luck sort them out. An oak does the opposite. It builds few, heavy, expensive seeds and gives each one a bank account, so the seedling can drive a root deep into the soil and survive its first dark summer under the canopy before it earns a single calorie from sunlight. That bank account is also the problem. A package of concentrated starch on the forest floor is exactly what every mouse, deer, bear, boar, jay, and squirrel is looking for. Oaks answer first with chemistry. Acorns are steeped in tannins, bitter compounds that bind proteins and make the nut difficult and unrewarding to digest in bulk. The defense is real but leaky. Plenty of animals eat acorns anyway, and people worked around it long ago. Across California, Native nations made acorn flour a staple for thousands of years by pounding the nuts and leaching them with water until the bitterness ran out. Korean kitchens still set leached acorn starch into a jelly called dotori-muk. The second defense is far stranger, because it is not a substance at all. It is a schedule. In most years an oak wood produces a moderate crop. Then, at irregular intervals, oaks across an entire region ripen a staggering number of acorns in the same autumn, a synchrony that can stretch for hundreds of miles. Ecologists call this masting, and the leading explanation is predator satiation: no population of seed eaters can consume a mast crop, so a share of the acorns survives simply by being uncountable. The strategy only works because of the lean years in between. Famine keeps the mouse and deer populations low, so when the flood finally comes there are too few mouths to meet it. An oak that fruited generously every single year would be feeding a permanent army. Then comes the twist. The animals that rob the oak are the same animals that plant it. Squirrels and jays are scatter-hoarders. They bury acorns one by one across the forest and fail to recover a large share of them. Each forgotten cache is a seed set at a useful depth, in open soil, away from the shade of its parent. Gray squirrels appear to sort their loot by species. White oak acorns germinate almost immediately in fall, which would ruin a winter store, so squirrels tend to eat those first, and some bite out the embryo before burying them, killing the seedling to preserve the meal. Red oak acorns stay dormant until spring, so they are cached whole. Blue jays go further, carrying as many as five acorns in a single flight and hiding them more than a mile from the tree that made them. Trees cannot walk. After the last ice age, oaks advanced north across the continent faster than any falling nut could travel, and many researchers credit jays with the journey. Set all of it beside the arithmetic and the scale becomes clear. A mature oak may release thousands of acorns in a single autumn and repeat that for two hundred years. Perhaps one of them, in all that time, becomes a tree that does the same. Everything else feeds the forest. That is not failure. That is the price of the ticket, and the oak has been paying it for tens of millions of years.
